# Cellulose vs Fiberglass Blown In Insulation: Blown-In Cellulose vs Fiberglass Compared

When comparing **cellulose vs fiberglass blown in insulation**, or weighing **blown-in cellulose vs fiberglass**, look beyond the material name. The location, condition of the area, product instructions and installation plan all matter. In San Antonio, a quote should explain what is being insulated, how even coverage will be achieved, and how the contractor will address existing air leaks or moisture concerns.

Cellulose and fiberglass are both used as loose-fill insulation, but they are not interchangeable in every application. A material’s performance depends in part on the product and how it is installed. Rather than assume one is always better, compare the proposed assembly and the details the contractor will verify.

## Start with the area being insulated

Ask the contractor to identify the exact part of the home included in the quote: an open attic floor, an enclosed wall, a sloped ceiling or another space. Each has different access and installation considerations. A loose-fill product intended for an open attic may need different handling or equipment when used in a closed cavity.

Ask for the product name and the manufacturer’s instructions for that application. Also confirm whether the work includes only adding insulation or preparing the area first. If you are comparing quotes, make sure they cover the same area and type of work.

The [U.S. Department of Energy’s guidance on blown insulation in existing attics](https://bsesc.energy.gov/energy-basics/blown-insulation-existing-attics) describes loose-fill cellulose and fiberglass as options for attic insulation. It also emphasizes even coverage, including at the top plates, and using baffles to keep insulation from blocking eaves. Baffles are barriers that preserve a path for attic ventilation where the roof and attic floor meet.

## Compare coverage and installation checks

Insulation works as part of a building assembly. Even a suitable material can leave weak spots if it is installed unevenly or misses edges and spaces around obstructions. Ask how the installer will handle the attic perimeter, framing, wiring, recessed fixtures and other obstacles. The answer should be specific to your home and the product being used.

Ask what installed depth or target R-value the quote specifies and how the contractor will check the result. R-value describes resistance to heat flow; it is not a guarantee of a particular energy bill or comfort outcome. Depth alone may not be enough to compare two products. Confirm that the proposed depth corresponds to the product’s installation instructions and stated performance.

A useful quote should identify the material, application and intended coverage, not just say “blown-in insulation.” If there are areas that cannot be reached or should not be covered, ask how those will be handled. For an existing attic, discuss whether old insulation will stay in place, be topped up or be removed, and why.

## Ask how the product accounts for settling

Loose-fill materials can settle, but the amount and how it is accounted for depend on the product and installation. Don’t assume a general statement about cellulose or fiberglass applies to every product. Ask whether the quoted depth is the initial installation depth or the depth used to represent the product’s settled performance.

The Department of Energy’s [Residential Energy Dynamics Calculator information](https://basc.pnnl.gov/redcalc/tool/loose-fill-insulation) explains that loose-fill calculations rely on product-specific information. That is one reason to compare like with like: ask for the product identification, specified coverage and installation basis in writing. If a contractor gives a target R-value, ask how it will be documented after installation.

## Understand moisture response and air sealing

Neither cellulose nor fiberglass should be treated as a fix for a roof leak, plumbing leak or other source of moisture. Before adding insulation, ask whether the attic or cavity is dry and whether there are signs of water entry or damaged materials. The Department of Energy’s [insulation guide](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-03/insulation_guide_0.pdf) discusses moisture concerns, including the need to avoid enclosing wet building materials and the potential for wet cellulose to lose thermal performance.

Insulation and air sealing are related but different jobs. Insulation slows heat flow; air sealing closes unintended openings that allow air to move through the building. Adding loose-fill insulation does not, by itself, seal every gap. Ask whether accessible ceiling penetrations and other air leaks will be addressed before new insulation is installed, and what work is included in the quote.

If insulation is damp, there is visible mold or rot, ventilation appears blocked, or wiring or other hazards are present, pause the insulation decision and seek a qualified evaluation. Don’t cover a condition that may need repair or specialist attention first.

## Make the quotes comparable

Before choosing, ask each contractor:

- What exact product and application are included?
- What area will be insulated, and what preparation is included?
- What installed depth or R-value is specified, and how will it be checked?
- How will the installer maintain even coverage around edges and obstructions?
- How is settling reflected in the specified depth?
- Will air sealing, moisture problems or existing insulation need attention first?
- How will attic ventilation paths be kept clear?

These questions make it easier to compare the complete installation rather than a material label or depth in isolation. A site-specific recommendation requires looking at the home and the area being insulated.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is cellulose or fiberglass always better for blown-in insulation?**

No. The right choice depends on the application, product specifications, condition of the space and quality of the installation. Compare the details of the proposed assembly rather than relying on a universal ranking.

**Does blown-in insulation seal air leaks?**

Not necessarily. Insulation slows heat flow, while air sealing closes gaps that allow air movement. Ask whether air sealing is included and which areas will be addressed.

**Can new loose-fill insulation go over existing insulation?**

It may be possible if the existing material and the area are suitable, but that requires an assessment. Wet, damaged or contaminated insulation and other attic concerns may need attention before new material is added.
